title: Onboarding drop off happens between the OTP and the first form field
summary: Most onboarding drop off happens between the OTP and the first form field. See why form abandonment peaks there and how prefill lifts completion.
body_markdown:

###


Key Takeaways


- The biggest onboarding drop off in most consumer fintech apps is not at KYC. It is the form that follows the OTP.
- Form abandonment peaks at the moment of highest intent, which is the worst possible place to charge a customer for their time.
- A verified Indian mobile number already carries a name, a profile and a behaviour history. Most flows treat it as a doorbell.
- Prefilling the form from the number, with risk signals returned in the same step, lifts completion for honest customers and flags risky ones earlier. That is what Mobile 360 does.


Most signup funnels lose people in the same place, and it is not where teams expect.


The phone number goes in. The OTP arrives and gets pasted. That step clears at a healthy rate. Then the form loads: full name as per PAN, date of birth, current address, pin code, PAN number, an occupation dropdown. The customer sees how long it runs and leaves. Not at KYC. Not at bank details. At the first empty field.


If you have looked at your own funnel, you have probably seen this shape. OTP conversion looks fine. The drop sits one screen later, at the box that says Name.


It is a strange place to lose someone. By the time they reach that box, you already have their phone number, and that number can tell you most of what the form is about to ask. You could know who they are before they type a word. Most onboarding flows ask them to type it anyway.


###


**Where onboarding drop off actually happens**


Teams tend to blame the heavy steps: document upload, selfie, bank account. Those do cost you people. But pull the funnel apart step by step and the steepest fall in most apps is earlier and quieter, between a successful OTP and the first completed field of the profile form.


The reason is simple once you see it. The OTP is a small win. The customer has just proven they want in. Then the app rewards that intent with eight empty fields, on a phone, often while they are doing something else. Every field is a small tax. Most people pay the first two and leave.

###


**What a verified phone number already knows**


A mobile number in India is not an anonymous string. It was issued against an ID. It has been used to open bank accounts, receive salary alerts, book cylinders, pay bills. Behind it sits a name, usually a date of birth, often an address, and a long trail of signals about how that number behaves.


Yet most onboarding flows use the number once, to ring it. Confirm someone answered, then ask the person at the door to write out who they are from scratch, as though the bell had told you nothing.


###


**How prefill changes in the flow**


This is the gap Mobile 360 closes. The customer types their number and verifies it with an OTP, same as today. Instead of a blank form, Mobile 360 returns a prefilled, verified profile built from what that number already knows about its owner. The customer’s job changes from typing to confirming: scan the fields, fix the odd one, tap next.


It does not replace digital KYC. DigiLocker, the selfie and the bank check run as they do now. What goes away is the typing that sits before KYC, which is exactly where the bus stop drop off lives.


The old journey: number, OTP, eight field form, document, selfie, bank account, done, if they are still there. With Mobile 360: number, OTP, confirm a profile that is already filled, selfie, bank account, done. The form the customer sees is already half complete, and the fields they touch are corrections, not compositions.


###


**The part that makes the risk team relax**


Prefill on its own is a conversion story. The reason Mobile 360 is not just autofill is what comes back with the profile.


Along with the name and the basics, the response carries the risk signals attached to the number: how long it has been live, whether it has been recycled, whether the name it carries matches the name the customer gave, and how the number behaves on the network. A fresh number with a mismatched name and a lot of spam in its contact graph is flagged before the customer has finished confirming their address. If you want the full list of what a number can tell you, we wrote it up in[Phone Risk Intelligence](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/phone-risk-intelligence/) .


So the same step that makes the honest customer’s form shorter makes the risky one’s profile visible. Product gets a faster funnel. Risk gets a signal at the top of it instead of a transaction monitor at the bottom. Nobody has to pick a side.


###


**What this looks like for a first time user**


For someone opening their first lending, investing or insurance account, on a phone, probably in a hurry, the difference between eight fields and confirm is the difference between finishing and leaving. The same logic is why we tell teams to[stop asking for bank details](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/verify-bank-account-without-asking-for-bank-details/) and prove the account with a ₹1 UPI tap instead. Every field you remove is the intent you keep.


For the business, the risk signals ride along in the same response. A risky number can be stepped up to a fuller check. A clean one goes straight through. The customer never sees which lane they were in.


###


**Why this matters for your business**


Every field you ask a customer to type is a tax on their intent, and most apps collect it at the exact moment intent peaks, right after the OTP. Mobile 360 spends that moment confirming instead of collecting.


If your funnel has a cliff between the OTP and the first form field, you already know roughly how many people are standing at the bottom of it. Mobile 360 is built for that cliff, and it happens to make the risky ones easier to spot on the way down.

###


**FAQs**


**Where does onboarding drop off usually happen?** In most consumer fintech apps, between a successful OTP and the first completed field of the profile form, before KYC or bank details.


**Why do customers abandon the onboarding form after the OTP?** Because the OTP feels like being in, and the form that follows asks for eight things they have to type on a phone. Intent is highest at that moment, and every field spends some of it.


**What is Mobile 360?** Cashfree Secure ID’s one step onboarding product. The customer verifies their phone number with an OTP and Mobile 360 returns a prefilled, verified profile along with the risk signals attached to that number.


**Does prefill replace digital KYC?** No. Mobile 360 removes the manual form filling that sits before KYC. DigiLocker, selfie and bank verification run as they do today.


**What risk signals come back with the profile?** Signals about the number itself: how long it has been active, whether it has been recycled, whether the name matches the one the customer gave, and how the number behaves on the network. Flagged numbers can be stepped up.


**Is customer consent part of the flow?** Yes. The customer verifies the number with an OTP and confirms the prefilled profile before anything proceeds, the same consent step they go through today.


**How do I measure whether prefill improved onboarding completion?** Compare completion from OTP success to profile submitted, before and after. That single step is where the lift shows up first.
